treatedConditionNote: Concern is the asthma and its control, not the inhaler; mild-to-moderate asthma is CACI-addressed.
faaStatusDescription:
FAA Asthma CACI lists it; rescue inhaler use no more than 2 times per week.

The FAA's CACI - Asthma Worksheet lists "Inhaled short-acting beta agonist (e.g., albuterol)" among its acceptable medications. For symptoms to count as "Stable and well-controlled", its criteria include "Frequency of symptoms - no more than 2 days per week", rescue inhaler use "no more than 2 times per week", "Use of oral corticosteroids for exacerbations - no more than 2 times per year", and in the last year "No in-patient hospitalizations" and no more than 2 outpatient clinic or urgent care visits for exacerbations, with symptoms fully resolved. Spirometry must be "Current within last 90 days", with FEV1 and FVC both at least 80% of predicted before bronchodilators. The worksheet lists monoclonal antibodies as not acceptable for CACI. "Spirometry is not required if the only treatment is PRN use on one or two days a week of a short-acting beta agonist (e.g., albuterol)."

"If the applicant meets ALL the acceptable certification criteria listed below, the AME can issue." The AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a clinic visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam", and "Applicants for first- or second- class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam." A short course of oral or injected steroids during a flare is acceptable, and "The AME must caution airman not to fly until course of oral steroids is completed and airman is symptom free."

That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.

faaStatusDescription:
Named on the FAA's breast cancer (in situ only) and Low T CACI worksheets.

Breast cancer. The FAA's CACI - Breast Cancer Worksheet names anastrozole (Arimidex) as an aromatase inhibitor under "Approved medications include:", with the criterion "An approved medication that is being well tolerated with no side effects". That worksheet covers only pathology showing "Carcinoma in Situ (Tis), Stage 0", "Ductal Carcinoma in Situ (DCIS)", "Lobular Carcinoma in Situ (LCIS)" or "Paget disease of the breast (Tis)", and it asks whether there is any evidence of "Stage IA or higher", "Invasive or metastatic disease" or "Use of chemotherapy for this condition at any time". The FAA's Breast Cancer disposition table sends chemotherapy, lymph node spread, metastatic disease or Stage IA or higher to DEFER: "Submit the information to the FAA for a possible Special Issuance." For non metastatic cancer with treatment completed 5 or more years ago, the table gives ISSUE "If no recurrence, current problems, or ongoing treatment" and adds "Continued hormone treatment is allowed (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitor)". Under the worksheet, the AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a clinic visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam", and "Applicants for first- or second-class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam."

Low testosterone. The FAA's Low Testosterone (Low T) Hypogonadism table lists Anastrozole on the row that says "See the CACI - Hypogonadism Worksheet." That worksheet's criteria include a stable condition with no side effects that would interfere with flight duties and a hematocrit of 54% or less.

That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.

The FAA's antihistamine table covers "All First-Generation Histamine-H1 receptor antagonist" as conditionally acceptable: "May be used occasionally (1-2 x per week) as a single agent or in any combination product", "NOT FOR DAILY USE". Its table, updated 09/30/2026, now lists brompheniramine individually, at 5 days.

Its Over-the-Counter guide places brompheniramine (Dimetapp) in the "AVOID" column among sedating antihistamines.

The FAA also requires the AME to warn that flight and safety-related duties are prohibited until after any applicable observation time.

New meds need a 48-hour ground trial; symptoms mean no flying.

The FAA's allergy table (updated 09/30/2026) lists this wait in its "Initial observation" column. Its Do Not Fly page says "pilots should not fly following the last dose of any medications until a period of time has elapsed equal to" five times the maximum pharmacologic half-life.

FAA policy, not a determination about you.

faaStatusDescription:
Asthma: both ingredients are on the FAA's CACI list. COPD isn't covered there.

For asthma, the FAA's CACI - Asthma Worksheet accepts "One or more of the following" medications and lists both "Inhaled long-acting beta agonist" and "Inhaled corticosteroid", by class rather than by drug name. For symptoms to count as "Stable and well-controlled", its criteria include "Frequency of symptoms - no more than 2 days per week", rescue inhaler use "no more than 2 times per week", "Use of oral corticosteroids for exacerbations - no more than 2 times per year", and in the last year "No in-patient hospitalizations" and no more than 2 outpatient clinic or urgent care visits for exacerbations, with symptoms fully resolved. Spirometry must be "Current within last 90 days", with FEV1 and FVC both at least 80% of predicted before bronchodilators. The worksheet lists monoclonal antibodies as not acceptable for CACI.

"If the applicant meets ALL the acceptable certification criteria listed below, the AME can issue." The AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a clinic visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam", and "Applicants for first- or second- class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam." A short course of oral or injected steroids during a flare is acceptable, and "The AME must caution airman not to fly until course of oral steroids is completed and airman is symptom free."

COPD is not addressed on that worksheet at all.

That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.

faaStatusDescription:
Arthritis/colitis CACI: 2-week ground trial, 4-hour no-fly after each dose.

FAA biologics list: "golimumab (Simponi)" under "Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) Blocking Agent".
No-fly after each dose: 4 hours.
First use: "All require a 2-week no-fly/ground trial" to verify no side effects.
Switching: "Changing from one biologic/biosimilar to another for the same indication requires a forty-eight (48) hour ground trial to mitigate any aeromedical risk."
Biosimilars: "FDA-approved biosimilars are also acceptable for any referenced brand name medication".
The table is headed "ACCEPTABLE BIOLOGICS - MONOTHERAPY MEDICATION".
It says: "Permitted if the underlying condition qualifies; consult the condition pages for details."
Arthritis worksheet: osteoarthritis, or autoimmune arthritis limited to "rheumatoid (limited to joint), psoriatic, or ankylosing spondylitis".
Colitis worksheet: a cause of "Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, microscopic colitis, or irritable bowel syndrome".
On each worksheet: "If the applicant meets ALL the acceptable certification criteria listed below, the AME can issue."
The AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam".
How often: annually for first or second class, and with each required exam for third class.

Source: FAA Biologics, Biosimilars, Non-Biologics, updated August 26, 2026; CACI Arthritis Worksheet, updated April 29, 2026; CACI Colitis Worksheet, updated April 29, 2026.

That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.

faaStatusDescription:
Arthritis CACI drug; the FAA asks for an eye-exam status summary.

Arthritis worksheet lists "Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ)/Chloroquine (Plaquenil/Aralen) see status report requirement below".
Criterion: "Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ)/ Chloroquine (CQ) Status Summary (Plaquenil/Aralen) is favorable and no concerns".
That form: "Please have the ophthalmologist or optometrist who monitors your medication provide the requested information in the space provided."
Arthritis worksheet: osteoarthritis, or autoimmune arthritis limited to "rheumatoid (limited to joint), psoriatic, or ankylosing spondylitis".
On the worksheet: "If the applicant meets ALL the acceptable certification criteria listed below, the AME can issue."
The AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam".
How often: annually for first or second class, and with each required exam for third class.

These FAA pages cover its use for arthritis.

faaStatusDescription:
Arthritis/colitis CACI: 2-week ground trial, 24-hour no-fly after each dose.

First use: "All require a 2-week no-fly/ground trial" to verify no side effects.

The AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam".
How often: annually for first or second class, and with each required exam for third class.

Source: FAA Biologics, Biosimilars, Non-Biologics, updated August 26, 2026; CACI Arthritis Worksheet, updated April 29, 2026; CACI Colitis Worksheet, updated April 29, 2026.

faaStatusDescription:
Hypothyroidism CACI drug; ALL worksheet criteria must be met.

CACI worksheet lists "liotrix (Thyrolar)" among acceptable medications.
Criteria: a normal TSH within the last year, the treating physician finds it stable with no changes recommended, and "None of the following: fatigue, mental status impairment, or symptoms related to pulmonary, cardiac, or visual systems".
For primary hypothyroidism meeting the worksheet, the FAA's table says ISSUE with no time limitation. It notes TSH up to 9.9 can be considered for CACI if other criteria are met.
It is DEFER if symptomatic, with "TSH 10 mIU/L or higher", or for central hypothyroidism.
If deferred, the FAA asks for a detailed Clinical Progress Note with a summary of the history, a TSH and other labs within 90 days, and copies of any imaging reports already performed.
The AME reviews a current Clinical Progress Note from a visit no more than 90 days before the exam, and a TSH.
How often: annually for first or second class, and with each required exam for third class.

Source: FAA Hypothyroidism table, updated January 25, 2023; CACI Hypothyroidism Worksheet, updated November 24, 2021.

faaStatusDescription:
Hypothyroidism CACI drug; ALL worksheet criteria must be met.

CACI worksheet lists "porcine thyroid (Armour)" among acceptable medications.
Criteria: a normal TSH within the last year, the treating physician finds it stable with no changes recommended, and "None of the following: fatigue, mental status impairment, or symptoms related to pulmonary, cardiac, or visual systems".
For primary hypothyroidism meeting the worksheet, the FAA's table says ISSUE with no time limitation. It notes TSH up to 9.9 can be considered for CACI if other criteria are met.
It is DEFER if symptomatic, with "TSH 10 mIU/L or higher", or for central hypothyroidism.
If deferred, the FAA asks for a detailed Clinical Progress Note with a summary of the history, a TSH and other labs within 90 days, and copies of any imaging reports already performed.
The AME reviews a current Clinical Progress Note from a visit no more than 90 days before the exam, and a TSH.
How often: annually for first or second class, and with each required exam for third class.

Source: FAA Hypothyroidism table, updated January 25, 2023; CACI Hypothyroidism Worksheet, updated November 24, 2021.

That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.

faaStatusDescription:
Conditional on a Special Issuance, and only as a single agent. The FAA lists it under "CONDITIONALLY Acceptable Antidepressant Medications with SI", "Used as a single agent, if otherwise qualified." It names the drug "citalopram (Celexa)".

On Item 47 the FAA states "The AME may not issue" and that "The Authorization decision is made on a case-by-case basis." Its criteria start with the diagnosis: "The applicant has one of the following diagnoses: Major depressive disorder (mild to moderate) either single episode or recurrent episode", "Dysthymic disorder", "Adjustment disorder with depressed mood", or "Any non-depression related condition for which the SSRI is used". Then "For a minimum of 3 continuous months prior, the applicant has been clinically stable as well as on a stable dose of medication without any aeromedically significant side effects and/or an increase in symptoms"; the medication must be one of the conditionally acceptable ones, "single use only; not in combination"; and the applicant "must be further evaluated by a Human Intervention Motivation Study (HIMS) AME." It also requires that "The applicant DOES NOT have symptoms or history of" psychosis, suicidal ideation, electro convulsive therapy, treatment with multiple SSRIs concurrently, or multi-agent drug protocol use.

Stopping the medication before an exam is its own path, not a shortcut. Where an airman "opts to discontinue use of the SSRI", the FAA says "the Examiner must notate in Block 60, Comments on History and Findings, on FAA Form 8500-8 and defer issuance", and to reapply for regular issuance the applicant "must be off the medication for a minimum of 60 days with a favorable report from the treating physician indicating stable mood and no aeromedically significant side effects".

The FAA renamed this pathway the Antidepressant Protocol; older references to an SSRI protocol are "considered encompassed in the Antidepressant Protocol".

Confirm against the current AME Guide and a qualified AME.

faaStatusDescription:
Conditional on a Special Issuance, and only as a single agent. The FAA lists it under "CONDITIONALLY Acceptable Antidepressant Medications with SI", "Used as a single agent, if otherwise qualified." It names the drug "desvenlafaxine (Pristiq)".

On Item 47 the FAA states "The AME may not issue" and that "The Authorization decision is made on a case-by-case basis." Its criteria start with the diagnosis: "The applicant has one of the following diagnoses: Major depressive disorder (mild to moderate) either single episode or recurrent episode", "Dysthymic disorder", "Adjustment disorder with depressed mood", or "Any non-depression related condition for which the SSRI is used". Then "For a minimum of 3 continuous months prior, the applicant has been clinically stable as well as on a stable dose of medication without any aeromedically significant side effects and/or an increase in symptoms"; the medication must be one of the conditionally acceptable ones, "single use only; not in combination"; and the applicant "must be further evaluated by a Human Intervention Motivation Study (HIMS) AME." It also requires that "The applicant DOES NOT have symptoms or history of" psychosis, suicidal ideation, electro convulsive therapy, treatment with multiple SSRIs concurrently, or multi-agent drug protocol use.

Stopping the medication before an exam is its own path, not a shortcut. Where an airman "opts to discontinue use of the SSRI", the FAA says "the Examiner must notate in Block 60, Comments on History and Findings, on FAA Form 8500-8 and defer issuance", and to reapply for regular issuance the applicant "must be off the medication for a minimum of 60 days with a favorable report from the treating physician indicating stable mood and no aeromedically significant side effects".

The FAA renamed this pathway the Antidepressant Protocol; older references to an SSRI protocol are "considered encompassed in the Antidepressant Protocol".

Confirm against the current AME Guide and a qualified AME.

faaStatusDescription:

The AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam".

faaStatusDescription:
Conditional on a Special Issuance, and only as a single agent. The FAA lists it under "CONDITIONALLY Acceptable Antidepressant Medications with SI", "Used as a single agent, if otherwise qualified." It names the drug "escitalopram (Lexapro)".

On Item 47 the FAA states "The AME may not issue" and that "The Authorization decision is made on a case-by-case basis." Its criteria start with the diagnosis: "The applicant has one of the following diagnoses: Major depressive disorder (mild to moderate) either single episode or recurrent episode", "Dysthymic disorder", "Adjustment disorder with depressed mood", or "Any non-depression related condition for which the SSRI is used". Then "For a minimum of 3 continuous months prior, the applicant has been clinically stable as well as on a stable dose of medication without any aeromedically significant side effects and/or an increase in symptoms"; the medication must be one of the conditionally acceptable ones, "single use only; not in combination"; and the applicant "must be further evaluated by a Human Intervention Motivation Study (HIMS) AME." It also requires that "The applicant DOES NOT have symptoms or history of" psychosis, suicidal ideation, electro convulsive therapy, treatment with multiple SSRIs concurrently, or multi-agent drug protocol use.

Stopping the medication before an exam is its own path, not a shortcut. Where an airman "opts to discontinue use of the SSRI", the FAA says "the Examiner must notate in Block 60, Comments on History and Findings, on FAA Form 8500-8 and defer issuance", and to reapply for regular issuance the applicant "must be off the medication for a minimum of 60 days with a favorable report from the treating physician indicating stable mood and no aeromedically significant side effects".

The FAA renamed this pathway the Antidepressant Protocol; older references to an SSRI protocol are "considered encompassed in the Antidepressant Protocol".

Confirm against the current AME Guide and a qualified AME.

faaStatusDescription:
Inhaled (Flovent): FAA Asthma CACI. Nasal (Flonase): allowed in MedGuide.

Inhaled for asthma (Flovent). The FAA's CACI - Asthma Worksheet lists "Inhaled corticosteroid" among its acceptable medications. For symptoms to count as "Stable and well-controlled", its criteria include "Frequency of symptoms - no more than 2 days per week", rescue inhaler use "no more than 2 times per week", "Use of oral corticosteroids for exacerbations - no more than 2 times per year", and in the last year "No in-patient hospitalizations" and no more than 2 outpatient clinic or urgent care visits for exacerbations, with symptoms fully resolved. Spirometry must be "Current within last 90 days", with FEV1 and FVC both at least 80% of predicted before bronchodilators. The worksheet lists monoclonal antibodies as not acceptable for CACI.

"If the applicant meets ALL the acceptable certification criteria listed below, the AME can issue." The AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a clinic visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam", and "Applicants for first- or second- class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam." A short course of oral or injected steroids during a flare is acceptable, and "The AME must caution airman not to fly until course of oral steroids is completed and airman is symptom free."

Asthma: both ingredients are on the FAA's CACI list. COPD isn't covered there.

For asthma, the FAA's CACI - Asthma Worksheet accepts "One or more of the following" medications and lists both "Inhaled corticosteroid" and "Inhaled long-acting beta agonist", by class rather than by drug name. For symptoms to count as "Stable and well-controlled", its criteria include "Frequency of symptoms - no more than 2 days per week", rescue inhaler use "no more than 2 times per week", "Use of oral corticosteroids for exacerbations - no more than 2 times per year", and in the last year "No in-patient hospitalizations" and no more than 2 outpatient clinic or urgent care visits for exacerbations, with symptoms fully resolved. Spirometry must be "Current within last 90 days", with FEV1 and FVC both at least 80% of predicted before bronchodilators. The worksheet lists monoclonal antibodies as not acceptable for CACI.

"If the applicant meets ALL the acceptable certification criteria listed below, the AME can issue." The AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a clinic visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam", and "Applicants for first- or second- class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam." A short course of oral or injected steroids during a flare is acceptable, and "The AME must caution airman not to fly until course of oral steroids is completed and airman is symptom free."

COPD is not addressed on that worksheet at all.

That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.

Acceptable types include "Open Angle being monitored and stable" and ocular hypertension or glaucoma suspect being monitored and stable.
Age at diagnosis: 40 or older. Intraocular pressure: 23 mm Hg or less in both eyes.

The FAA's CACI - Breast Cancer Worksheet names letrozole (Femara) as an aromatase inhibitor under "Approved medications include:", with the criterion "An approved medication that is being well tolerated with no side effects". That worksheet covers only pathology showing "Carcinoma in Situ (Tis), Stage 0", "Ductal Carcinoma in Situ (DCIS)", "Lobular Carcinoma in Situ (LCIS)" or "Paget disease of the breast (Tis)", and it asks whether there is any evidence of "Stage IA or higher", "Invasive or metastatic disease" or "Use of chemotherapy for this condition at any time". The FAA's Breast Cancer disposition table sends chemotherapy, lymph node spread, metastatic disease or Stage IA or higher to DEFER: "Submit the information to the FAA for a possible Special Issuance." For non metastatic cancer with treatment completed 5 or more years ago, the table gives ISSUE "If no recurrence, current problems, or ongoing treatment" and adds "Continued hormone treatment is allowed (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitor)". Under the worksheet, the AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a clinic visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam", and "Applicants for first- or second-class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam."

Polycystic ovarian syndrome. The FAA's CACI - Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) Worksheet lists letrozole among the medications that "May be used in combination", with a treating physician finding the condition "Stable on current regimen" and "No side effects from medication".

faaStatusDescription:

The AME reviews a current Clinical Progress Note from a visit no more than 90 days before the exam, and a TSH.
How often: annually for first or second class, and with each required exam for third class.

faaStatusDescription:
The FAA's answer depends on whether you have a diagnosis of diabetes, not on the brand.

With a diagnosis of diabetes the diabetes pathway applies even when the prescription is for weight loss: the FAA writes "If used for DIABETES, see www.faa.gov/go/diabetic", and there the AME defers at initial certification.

With no diagnosis of diabetes, taken for weight loss, the FAA lists liraglutide under "ACCEPTABLE Weight Loss Medications", "When certification criteria are met", with a CACI worksheet the AME can work from.

There is a third path the FAA keeps separate: it says "See either the Prediabetes or Weight Loss Management disposition tables", and its worksheet notes "If A1c is in the prediabetic range (5.7 to 6.4%)" to "see the Pre-Diabetes page".

If your A1c sits in that band, that is the page your AME works from, not this one. Victoza is usually the diabetes product and Saxenda the weight loss one, but your diagnosis is what decides which entry applies to you.

faaStatusDescription:
Taken for type 2 diabetes, the FAA's disposition is DEFER, "Submit the information to the FAA." It records this as "Initial Special Issuance – Requires FAA Decision". That is its listed disposition for "Treated with one or more (non-insulin) diabetic medications". The same disposition cell continues "Follow up Special Issuances - See Diabetes Mellitus - Type II, Medication Controlled (Not Insulin)", a different path from the initial decision.

Its Acceptable Combinations chart places liraglutide in Group D (GLP1 mimetics) and says "Only ONE Medication allowed from each group (A–G)". Starting a "Group C - G" medication carries a 30-day observation, and a dose or formulation change "Within Group B-G" carries 48 hours. The chart also marks Group D as not allowed with Meglitinides. The chart carries the FAA's own note that "ALL medication Group Letters have been updated", so an older copy will not match. Adding it to an established regimen ("on Group A - G" plus a "new Group B - G" medication) carries a 14-day observation.

treatedConditionNote: The FAA's concern is the condition being treated, not the drug. This entry is the weight loss indication, with no diagnosis of diabetes. If you have a diabetes diagnosis, the FAA's diabetes protocol applies to you and not this page. If you take it for prediabetes, insulin resistance or metabolic syndrome, the FAA works from a separate "CACI - Prediabetes Worksheet" covering "Metabolic Syndrome, Impaired Fasting Glucose, Insulin Resistance, Glucose Elevation/Intolerance", with its own Block 60 statement, "CACI qualified prediabetes". That page, not this one.
faaStatusDescription:
"When certification criteria are met", the FAA lists liraglutide under "ACCEPTABLE Weight Loss Medications". It names no brand for it.

Its criteria: "A1C must be 6.4 or less with no diagnosis of diabetes", "No history of hypoglycemia requiring intervention", and "One (1) week after starting for weight loss." It also requires "48-hour observation with each dose increase, medication, or formulation change." There is a third path the FAA keeps separate: it says "See either the Prediabetes or Weight Loss Management disposition tables", and its worksheet notes "If A1c is in the prediabetic range (5.7 to 6.4%)" to "see the Pre-Diabetes page".

If your A1c sits in that band, that is the page your AME works from, not this one.

The page also accepts a GLP-1 agonist combined with orlistat: "orlistat + GLP-1 agonist", with "only one diabetic medication".

Its Weight Loss Management disposition table is ISSUE on ONE non-insulin diabetic medication component, and on "TWO (2) or more" it is DEFER, "Submit the information to the FAA for a possible Special Issuance".

Even the ISSUE is not automatic: it "requires a current, detailed Clinical Progress Note from the treating physician and Hemoglobin A1c lab performed no more than 90 days before the AME exam", or a "Weight Loss Management Status Report".

Its CACI worksheet takes "ONLY ONE of the medications listed", says "If the applicant has EVER had an A1C OF 6.5% OR GREATER, DO NOT USE THIS CACI." and that "Diabetes in remission (diet-controlled), diabetes treated with medication (including insulin), or diabetes insipidus DO NOT qualify for this CACI." "Applicants for first or second- class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam."

It notes a "'Hang-over effect' morning after safety concern" and that "Taking melatonin at the wrong time can actually worsen jetlag and cause daytime drowsiness."

Its sleep aids page covers the class: "All the currently available sleep aids, both prescription and over the counter, can cause impairment of mental processes and reaction times, even when the individual feels fully awake." That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.

treatedConditionNote: Concern is the asthma/allergy and its control, not the drug.
faaStatusDescription:
On the FAA's Asthma CACI list and its ACCEPTABLE allergy medication list.

For asthma, the FAA's CACI - Asthma Worksheet lists "leukotriene receptor antagonist, (e.g. montelukast [Singulair])" among its acceptable medications. For symptoms to count as "Stable and well-controlled", its criteria include "Frequency of symptoms - no more than 2 days per week", rescue inhaler use "no more than 2 times per week", "Use of oral corticosteroids for exacerbations - no more than 2 times per year", and in the last year "No in-patient hospitalizations" and no more than 2 outpatient clinic or urgent care visits for exacerbations, with symptoms fully resolved. Spirometry must be "Current within last 90 days", with FEV1 and FVC both at least 80% of predicted before bronchodilators. The worksheet lists monoclonal antibodies as not acceptable for CACI.

"If the applicant meets ALL the acceptable certification criteria listed below, the AME can issue." The AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a clinic visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam", and "Applicants for first- or second- class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam." A short course of oral or injected steroids during a flare is acceptable, and "The AME must caution airman not to fly until course of oral steroids is completed and airman is symptom free."

For allergy, its Allergy - Antihistamine & Immunotherapy Medication page lists "Oral: montelukast (Singulair)" under "ACCEPTABLE* (Non-Sedating) Antihistamine and Allergy Medications", and says "Airmen who are exhibiting symptoms, regardless of the treatment used, must not fly." A new medication carries a "Mandatory 48-hour ground trial required after initial use."

That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.

For that table the FAA writes that "All medications listed below may cause sedation or drowsiness, impairing cognitive function and seriously degrading pilot performance.", that "AMEs should caution pilots on use and provide additional No Fly wait times where applicable." and that "If applicant is using the following medications routinely, AMEs should DEFER." Its general rule is a no-fly interval of five times the medication's maximum pharmacologic half-life.

That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.

faaStatusDescription:

faaStatusDescription:
The FAA's answer depends on whether you have a diagnosis of diabetes, not on the brand.

With a diagnosis of diabetes the diabetes pathway applies even when the prescription is for weight loss: the FAA writes "If used for DIABETES, see www.faa.gov/go/diabetic", and there the AME defers at initial certification.

With no diagnosis of diabetes, taken for weight loss, the FAA lists semaglutide under "ACCEPTABLE Weight Loss Medications", "When certification criteria are met", with a CACI worksheet the AME can work from.

There is a third path the FAA keeps separate: it says "See either the Prediabetes or Weight Loss Management disposition tables", and its worksheet notes "If A1c is in the prediabetic range (5.7 to 6.4%)" to "see the Pre-Diabetes page".

If your A1c sits in that band, that is the page your AME works from, not this one. Ozempic and Rybelsus are usually the diabetes products and Wegovy the weight loss one, but your diagnosis is what decides which entry applies to you.

FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners: Diabetes Mellitus disposition table, All Classes (updated 09/27/2023), row B; Acceptable Combinations of Diabetes Medications (updated 08/26/2026)

faaStatusDescription:
Taken for type 2 diabetes, the FAA's disposition is DEFER, "Submit the information to the FAA." It records this as "Initial Special Issuance – Requires FAA Decision". That is its listed disposition for "Treated with one or more (non-insulin) diabetic medications". The same disposition cell continues "Follow up Special Issuances - See Diabetes Mellitus - Type II, Medication Controlled (Not Insulin)", a different path from the initial decision.

Its Acceptable Combinations chart places semaglutide in Group D (GLP1 mimetics) and says "Only ONE Medication allowed from each group (A–G)". Starting a "Group C - G" medication carries a 30-day observation, and a dose or formulation change "Within Group B-G" carries 48 hours. The chart also marks Group D as not allowed with Meglitinides. The chart carries the FAA's own note that "ALL medication Group Letters have been updated", so an older copy will not match. Adding it to an established regimen ("on Group A - G" plus a "new Group B - G" medication) carries a 14-day observation.

treatedConditionNote: The FAA's concern is the condition being treated, not the drug. This entry is the weight loss indication, with no diagnosis of diabetes. If you have a diabetes diagnosis, the FAA's diabetes protocol applies to you and not this page. If you take it for prediabetes, insulin resistance or metabolic syndrome, the FAA works from a separate "CACI - Prediabetes Worksheet" covering "Metabolic Syndrome, Impaired Fasting Glucose, Insulin Resistance, Glucose Elevation/Intolerance", with its own Block 60 statement, "CACI qualified prediabetes". That page, not this one.
faaStatusDescription:
"When certification criteria are met", the FAA lists Wegovy under "ACCEPTABLE Weight Loss Medications".

It names it "semaglutide (Wegovy) [injection or oral]".

Its criteria: "A1C must be 6.4 or less with no diagnosis of diabetes", "No history of hypoglycemia requiring intervention", and "One (1) week after starting for weight loss." It also requires "48-hour observation with each dose increase, medication, or formulation change." There is a third path the FAA keeps separate: it says "See either the Prediabetes or Weight Loss Management disposition tables", and its worksheet notes "If A1c is in the prediabetic range (5.7 to 6.4%)" to "see the Pre-Diabetes page".

If your A1c sits in that band, that is the page your AME works from, not this one.

The page also accepts a GLP-1 agonist combined with orlistat: "orlistat + GLP-1 agonist", with "only one diabetic medication".

Its Weight Loss Management disposition table is ISSUE on ONE non-insulin diabetic medication component, and on "TWO (2) or more" it is DEFER, "Submit the information to the FAA for a possible Special Issuance".

Even the ISSUE is not automatic: it "requires a current, detailed Clinical Progress Note from the treating physician and Hemoglobin A1c lab performed no more than 90 days before the AME exam", or a "Weight Loss Management Status Report".

Its CACI worksheet takes "ONLY ONE of the medications listed", says "If the applicant has EVER had an A1C OF 6.5% OR GREATER, DO NOT USE THIS CACI." and that "Diabetes in remission (diet-controlled), diabetes treated with medication (including insulin), or diabetes insipidus DO NOT qualify for this CACI." "Applicants for first or second- class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam."

faaStatusDescription:
Conditional on a Special Issuance, and only as a single agent. The FAA lists it under "CONDITIONALLY Acceptable Antidepressant Medications with SI", "Used as a single agent, if otherwise qualified." It names the drug "sertraline (Zoloft)".

On Item 47 the FAA states "The AME may not issue" and that "The Authorization decision is made on a case-by-case basis." Its criteria start with the diagnosis: "The applicant has one of the following diagnoses: Major depressive disorder (mild to moderate) either single episode or recurrent episode", "Dysthymic disorder", "Adjustment disorder with depressed mood", or "Any non-depression related condition for which the SSRI is used". Then "For a minimum of 3 continuous months prior, the applicant has been clinically stable as well as on a stable dose of medication without any aeromedically significant side effects and/or an increase in symptoms"; the medication must be one of the conditionally acceptable ones, "single use only; not in combination"; and the applicant "must be further evaluated by a Human Intervention Motivation Study (HIMS) AME." It also requires that "The applicant DOES NOT have symptoms or history of" psychosis, suicidal ideation, electro convulsive therapy, treatment with multiple SSRIs concurrently, or multi-agent drug protocol use.

Stopping the medication before an exam is its own path, not a shortcut. Where an airman "opts to discontinue use of the SSRI", the FAA says "the Examiner must notate in Block 60, Comments on History and Findings, on FAA Form 8500-8 and defer issuance", and to reapply for regular issuance the applicant "must be off the medication for a minimum of 60 days with a favorable report from the treating physician indicating stable mood and no aeromedically significant side effects".

The FAA renamed this pathway the Antidepressant Protocol; older references to an SSRI protocol are "considered encompassed in the Antidepressant Protocol".

Confirm against the current AME Guide and a qualified AME.

Breast cancer. The FAA's CACI - Breast Cancer Worksheet names tamoxifen (Nolvadex) under "Approved medications include:", with the criterion "An approved medication that is being well tolerated with no side effects". That worksheet covers only pathology showing "Carcinoma in Situ (Tis), Stage 0", "Ductal Carcinoma in Situ (DCIS)", "Lobular Carcinoma in Situ (LCIS)" or "Paget disease of the breast (Tis)", and it asks whether there is any evidence of "Stage IA or higher", "Invasive or metastatic disease" or "Use of chemotherapy for this condition at any time". Under the worksheet, the AME reviews a Clinical Progress Note from a clinic visit "no more than 90 days prior to the AME exam", and "Applicants for first- or second-class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam."

Low testosterone. The FAA's Low Testosterone (Low T) Hypogonadism table lists Tamoxifen on the row that says "See the CACI - Hypogonadism Worksheet." That worksheet's criteria include a stable condition with no side effects that would interfere with flight duties and a hematocrit of 54% or less.

faaStatusDescription:
The FAA's answer depends on whether you have a diagnosis of diabetes, not on the brand.

With a diagnosis of diabetes the diabetes pathway applies even when the prescription is for weight loss: the FAA writes "If used for DIABETES, see www.faa.gov/go/diabetic", and there the AME defers at initial certification.

With no diagnosis of diabetes, taken for weight loss, the FAA lists tirzepatide under "ACCEPTABLE Weight Loss Medications", "When certification criteria are met", with a CACI worksheet the AME can work from.

There is a third path the FAA keeps separate: it says "See either the Prediabetes or Weight Loss Management disposition tables", and its worksheet notes "If A1c is in the prediabetic range (5.7 to 6.4%)" to "see the Pre-Diabetes page".

If your A1c sits in that band, that is the page your AME works from, not this one. Mounjaro is usually the diabetes product and Zepbound the weight loss one, but your diagnosis is what decides which entry applies to you.

faaStatusDescription:
Taken for type 2 diabetes, the FAA's disposition is DEFER, "Submit the information to the FAA." It records this as "Initial Special Issuance – Requires FAA Decision". That is its listed disposition for "Treated with one or more (non-insulin) diabetic medications". The same disposition cell continues "Follow up Special Issuances - See Diabetes Mellitus - Type II, Medication Controlled (Not Insulin)", a different path from the initial decision.

Its Acceptable Combinations chart places tirzepatide in Group D, in its GLP-1 / GIP box alongside the GLP1 mimetics, and says "Only ONE Medication allowed from each group (A–G)". Starting a "Group C - G" medication carries a 30-day observation, and a dose or formulation change "Within Group B-G" carries 48 hours. The chart also marks Group D as not allowed with Meglitinides. The chart carries the FAA's own note that "ALL medication Group Letters have been updated", so an older copy will not match. Adding it to an established regimen ("on Group A - G" plus a "new Group B - G" medication) carries a 14-day observation.

If you take it for prediabetes, insulin resistance or metabolic syndrome, the FAA works from a separate "CACI - Prediabetes Worksheet" covering "Metabolic Syndrome, Impaired Fasting Glucose, Insulin Resistance, Glucose Elevation/Intolerance", with its own Block 60 statement, "CACI qualified prediabetes". faaStatusDescription:
"When certification criteria are met", the FAA lists Zepbound under "ACCEPTABLE Weight Loss Medications".

It names it "tirzepatide (Zepbound) [GIP + GLP-1 Agonist]".

Its criteria: "A1C must be 6.4 or less with no diagnosis of diabetes", "No history of hypoglycemia requiring intervention", and "One (1) week after starting for weight loss." It also requires "48-hour observation with each dose increase, medication, or formulation change." There is a third path the FAA keeps separate: it says "See either the Prediabetes or Weight Loss Management disposition tables", and its worksheet notes "If A1c is in the prediabetic range (5.7 to 6.4%)" to "see the Pre-Diabetes page".

If your A1c sits in that band, that is the page your AME works from, not this one.

The page also accepts a GLP-1 agonist combined with orlistat: "orlistat + GLP-1 agonist", with "only one diabetic medication".

Its Weight Loss Management disposition table is ISSUE on ONE non-insulin diabetic medication component, and on "TWO (2) or more" it is DEFER, "Submit the information to the FAA for a possible Special Issuance".

Even the ISSUE is not automatic: it "requires a current, detailed Clinical Progress Note from the treating physician and Hemoglobin A1c lab performed no more than 90 days before the AME exam", or a "Weight Loss Management Status Report".

Its CACI worksheet takes "ONLY ONE of the medications listed", says "If the applicant has EVER had an A1C OF 6.5% OR GREATER, DO NOT USE THIS CACI." and that "Diabetes in remission (diet-controlled), diabetes treated with medication (including insulin), or diabetes insipidus DO NOT qualify for this CACI." "Applicants for first or second- class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam."

faaStatusDescription:
Conditional on a Special Issuance, and only as a single agent. The FAA lists it under "CONDITIONALLY Acceptable Antidepressant Medications with SI", "Used as a single agent, if otherwise qualified." It names the drug "venlafaxine (Effexor)".

On Item 47 the FAA states "The AME may not issue" and that "The Authorization decision is made on a case-by-case basis." Its criteria start with the diagnosis: "The applicant has one of the following diagnoses: Major depressive disorder (mild to moderate) either single episode or recurrent episode", "Dysthymic disorder", "Adjustment disorder with depressed mood", or "Any non-depression related condition for which the SSRI is used". Then "For a minimum of 3 continuous months prior, the applicant has been clinically stable as well as on a stable dose of medication without any aeromedically significant side effects and/or an increase in symptoms"; the medication must be one of the conditionally acceptable ones, "single use only; not in combination"; and the applicant "must be further evaluated by a Human Intervention Motivation Study (HIMS) AME." It also requires that "The applicant DOES NOT have symptoms or history of" psychosis, suicidal ideation, electro convulsive therapy, treatment with multiple SSRIs concurrently, or multi-agent drug protocol use.

Stopping the medication before an exam is its own path, not a shortcut. Where an airman "opts to discontinue use of the SSRI", the FAA says "the Examiner must notate in Block 60, Comments on History and Findings, on FAA Form 8500-8 and defer issuance", and to reapply for regular issuance the applicant "must be off the medication for a minimum of 60 days with a favorable report from the treating physician indicating stable mood and no aeromedically significant side effects".

The FAA renamed this pathway the Antidepressant Protocol; older references to an SSRI protocol are "considered encompassed in the Antidepressant Protocol".

Confirm against the current AME Guide and a qualified AME.

treatedConditionNote: The FAA's concern is the condition requiring anticoagulation (e.g., clot, arrhythmia), not the drug alone.
faaStatusDescription:
FAA: 6 weeks' observation and 6 INRs after starting; monthly INRs after that.

The FAA's Anticoagulants page names warfarin (Jantoven). "For applicants who are just beginning warfarin (Jantoven) treatment the following is required: Minimum observation time of 6 weeks after initiation of warfarin therapy; Must also meet any required observation time for the underlying condition; AND 6 INRs, no more frequently than 1 per week". For established use, the "status report from the treating physician should address and include: Drug dose history and schedule; Comment regarding side effects; AND A minimum of monthly International Normalized Ratio (INRs) results for the immediate prior 6 months."

For carotid or vertebral artery stenosis, its CACI worksheet notes "DOAC/NOAC/coumadin do not qualify for CACI". Its AASI for venous thromboembolism tells the examiner to defer if more than 20% of INR values on warfarin are below 2.0 or above 3.0.

That is what the FAA publishes, not a determination about you.
